Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

There were nine volunteers on the rota, but only seven were standing by the time the kettle boiled because Jo was still on the bus and Martin had called to say his child was sick. The hall manager had left the side entrance unlocked and put the key in a blue mug by the sign-in sheet. The first job was checking the delivery crates against the paper list and making space in the walk-in fridge.

Leila was supervising the hot line, and she had written the menu on a piece of brown card: lentil soup, rice with roasted carrots, and apples in paper bags for the children who came with parents. She said, “The soup needs to stay mild because some of the older guests cannot manage much pepper.” Then she pointed out that the large pot had been used for tomato sauce the night before, so we rinsed it twice and checked the rim for dried sauce. The kitchen smelled of coffee and wet wool, and the floor near the back sink needed another mop before anyone carried the bread through.

Our delivery driver had left four boxes of bread, two crates of carrots, a sack of onions, and a small insulated tub with no label on top of it. The slip said the tub contained oat milk, but the lid was not fully closed, so Leila asked us to keep it on the lower shelf until we could ask the driver about the seal. There was also a note from the garden group saying their herbs were delayed and might arrive after eleven. The soup recipe did not depend on fresh herbs, but Leila wanted parsley on the rice if it arrived before we started serving.

For the morning jobs, the list went like this:
1. Check the temperature of the fridge and write it on the clipboard.
2. Count the paper bowls and spoons and leave one bundle near the hall entrance.
3. Wash the carrots before they go to the roasting trays.

I checked the fridge display, and it read three degrees. Then I wrote the reading beside the date on the sheet. We had two hundred paper bowls, which was enough for the expected crowd, but there were only a hundred and eighty spoons, so we put one extra box on the shopping note. The carrots came in with a little soil still on them, and their green tops had already been trimmed.

At seven twenty, Jo arrived with her yellow raincoat over one arm and apologized for the bus running slowly. She took the apple station and asked whether we had enough clean paper bags for the school families. There were two full rolls in the cupboard and a half roll in the drawer, so I told her that should cover the first wave. She arranged the apples by size because the smaller ones fit better into the bags and set a handwritten card beside them that said, “Please take one for each child.” Jo said the card had been useful last week when a few people thought the apples were only for volunteers.

We kept the serving tables against the long window because the hall had a repair crew coming to inspect the heating panel in the afternoon. The manager had asked us not to cover the small access door beside the radiator, and Leila marked a clear path on the floor with two strips of yellow tape. If the repair crew arrived before lunch, we were to leave the door open and move the clean trays to the other end of the table. That condition mattered later because the heating technician called at ten thirty and said he would come through the kitchen rather than the main entrance.

At eight, the bread volunteer noticed one box was damp at the bottom, but the loaves inside were wrapped and still dry, so we set that box on a separate trolley and asked the manager to check the cardboard before the next shift. A guest named Mr. Bell came early and asked if he could sit by the window while he waited for his sister. I said the tables were not open yet, but brought him a mug of tea, and he said that was kind and he would wait near the coat hooks. He had a folded bus timetable in his pocket and kept checking the time because his sister was coming from the clinic.

At nine fifteen, I finished the count of the meal cards and found thirty-eight blue cards for guests and twelve green cards for the volunteer meal. Leila said not to mix them because the kitchen records the guest count separately from the staff count. I clipped the blue stack to the front of the clipboard and put the green cards in an envelope beside the tea tin. The printer in the office had run out of ink, so we copied the allergy note by hand. The note said the rice contained no nuts, but the soup had been made beside a tray of sesame rolls, and guests who asked about allergies should speak with Leila rather than relying on the menu card.

When the garden group finally arrived at ten fifty, they brought a paper bag of parsley and a small bunch of chives, but no basil because the plants had been damaged in the rain. We washed the parsley in the clean sink, and Leila chopped half of it for the rice while saving the rest in a covered bowl. She asked me to forward the updated serving plan to the evening coordinator before I left, and I said I would include the note about the technician and the extra spoons so the next team could see what had changed. The coordinator had requested one message before noon and had not asked us to send the guest names.

After the first serving wave, the technician came through the kitchen and waited while we moved two trays away from the access door. He checked the panel without asking anyone to switch off the ovens and said the sound from the fan was normal. He left a printed appointment slip on the manager's desk for a return visit next Thursday. By then, the soup pot was nearly empty and the rice still covered one tray. Leila asked us to keep the last apples for the families arriving from the clinic rather than putting them out with the general fruit, and Jo placed the remaining bags beside the blue meal cards."}]
